title: Delhi HC Lets NCR Lawyers and Court Staff Bring Non-BS-VI Cars In on Hearing Days
meta_description: Delhi High Court carves out a narrow exemption from its winter vehicle ban, letting NCR advocates and court staff drive in on hearing days only.
case_name: Delhi High Court Bar Association v. Government of NCT of Delhi & Ors.
body: On 6 November 2026, Justice Amit Mahajan of the Delhi High Court gave the Delhi High Court Bar Association a narrow win in its challenge to the capital's winter ban on vehicles registered outside Delhi. The order does not touch the ban itself. It carves out a limited exemption for advocates and court staff who need to drive into the city to attend hearings.

The ban traces to a notification dated 23 June 2026 issued by the Department of Environment and Forests, Government of NCT of Delhi. It stops vehicles registered outside Delhi that do not meet BS-VI emission norms from entering the city between 1 November 2026 and 31 January 2027, a stretch when pollution levels in the capital typically worsen. DHCBA did not ask the court to strike down this restriction. Its petition was narrower: a large number of its members, along with court staff, live in Noida, Gurugram, Ghaziabad and Faridabad because housing in Delhi itself is expensive, and many of them drive vehicles that fall short of BS-VI standards. A blanket ban, the Association argued, would keep them from reaching the Delhi High Court and the district courts at Saket, Tis Hazari, Patiala House, Karkardooma, Dwarka and Rohini on days they are required to appear.

Justice Mahajan accepted that framing. Attending court to assist in judicial work, the order records, is an essential function that cannot be disrupted overnight by a restriction aimed at commercial and private traffic generally. The relief granted reflects that reasoning rather than any broader finding on the environmental merits of the ban. Advocates and court staff based in the National Capital Region may now bring their vehicles into Delhi, but only on days the courts are functioning, and only if the vehicle carries a valid parking sticker issued by a recognised Bar Association in Delhi. Anyone stopped while exercising the exemption must be able to produce identification establishing that they are, in fact, an advocate or court employee covered by the order.

The scope of the relief is worth being precise about, since reports have used different shorthand for it. This is not a general exemption for lawyers' cars at all times, and it is not a suspension of the underlying notification. It is a court-day pass, tied to the purpose of attending hearings, and conditioned on proof of identity and a valid sticker. Reports note that a detailed order was still awaited at the time of the hearing, so the mechanics of how stickers will be checked and renewed may be spelled out further once that order is released.

This ruling sits alongside a separate and so far unsuccessful challenge to the same winter restriction. Earlier the same week, a Division Bench of Acting Chief Justice Nitin Wasudeo Sambre and Justice Sanjay Sharma declined to stay the ban in a different petition, issued notice to the authorities, and listed that matter for 27 November 2026. Read together, the two orders leave the restriction itself intact for everyone else while giving one defined category of road users, people whose attendance keeps the court system running, a way to keep appearing for hearings through the winter months.

For businesses and transport operators with vehicles registered outside Delhi, nothing changes. The ban continues to apply in full between now and the end of January, and the exemption carved out this week is specific to advocates and court staff carrying out court-related duties. Firms that depend on vehicles crossing into Delhi from Noida, Gurugram or Ghaziabad during this period should plan around the restriction rather than assume any relief will extend to them, since the order is addressed squarely to the administration of justice and not to commerce generally.

What the order does illustrate is a court weighing a specific, provable disruption, lawyers and staff unable to reach hearings, against a general public health measure, and finding room for a conditional, time-bound accommodation rather than either upholding the ban without exception or suspending it altogether. That kind of calibrated relief, tied closely to the facts a petitioner can show rather than to the policy question at large, is likely to come up again as other categories of NCR commuters bring similar petitions before the winter restriction lifts at the end of January.
why_it_matters: The ban on non-BS-VI vehicles registered outside Delhi stays in force through 31 January 2027, and this order does not change that for ordinary commuters, transporters or businesses. It matters specifically to advocates and court staff based in Noida, Gurugram, Ghaziabad and Faridabad, who can now drive into Delhi on hearing days if they carry a valid Bar Association parking sticker and identification. Clients and firms relying on NCR-based counsel for Delhi litigation should confirm their lawyers and support staff are aware of the sticker requirement so attendance at hearings is not disrupted this winter.
card_summary: Delhi High Court lets NCR-based advocates and court staff drive non-BS-VI vehicles into Delhi on hearing days only, while the broader winter entry ban for everyone else stays in force through January 2027.
card_tip: If your Delhi litigation team commutes from Noida, Gurugram or Ghaziabad, confirm they carry a valid Bar Association parking sticker and identification before driving in on hearing days this winter.
